'''Spuyten Duyvil''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|s|p|aɪ|t|ən|_|ˈ|d|aɪ|v|əl}}, {{respell|SPY-tən|DY-vəl}}<ref>Merims, Belden. [https://books.google.com/books?id=8Y0wFVusZEIC&q=spuyten+duyvil+pronounced ''Newcomer's Handbook for Moving to New York City''], p. 63. First Books, 2001. {{ISBN|9780912301488}}. Accessed November 5, 2020. "Spuyten Duyvil (pronounced SPY-ten DIE-vul) has a southward pitch, so it seems to look back at Manhattan, but if you live here you're sure to look west to the spectacular sunsets, which blaze and bleed over the river."</ref>) is a neighborhood of [[the Bronx]], [[New York City]]. It is bounded on the north by [[Riverdale, Bronx|Riverdale]], on the east by [[Kingsbridge, Bronx|Kingsbridge]], on the south by the [[Harlem River]], and on the west by the [[Hudson River]].<ref name=encnyc>Wolfe, Gerald R. "Spuyten Duyvil neighborhood" in {{harvnb|Jackson|1995|p=1224}}</ref> Some consider it to be the southernmost part of Riverdale.<ref name=aia>{{harvnb|White|Willensky|Leadon|2010|p=868}}</ref>

==Etymology==
{{further|Spuyten Duyvil Creek#Etymology}}

The area is named after [[Spuyten Duyvil Creek]]. "Spuyten Duyvil" may be literally translated as "Spouting Devil" or ''Spuitende Duivel'' in [[Dutch language|Dutch]], a reference to the strong and wild tidal currents found at that location.  It may also be translated as "Spewing Devil" or "Spinning Devil", or more loosely as "Devil's Whirlpool" or "Devil's Spate." ''Spui'' is a Dutch word involving outlets for water.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=0KhIAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA106 ''Sixteenth Annual Report, 1911, of the American Secneic and Historic Preservation Society to the Legislature of the State of New York ''], p. 106. [[American Scenic and Historic Preservation Society]], 1911. Accessed November 4, 2015. "Another reason is that there are phonetic elements in the name as first written which suggest other meanings quite appropriate to the locality. There is a Dutch word 'spui' of frequent use in Holland, meaning a sluice way or canal. The Spui at The Hague, part of which is redeemed and used as a street, is a famous thoroughfare."</ref><ref name="NYCPks-SpuytenDuyvilCrk">{{cite web|title=Inwood Hill Park: Spuyten Duyvil Creek|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/inwood-hill-park/highlights/8272|publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]]|access-date=2 January 2017}}</ref><ref name="NYPL-SpuytenDuyvil-Ap2010">{{cite news|last1=McDonald|first1=Rabecca|title=History of the Name Spuyten Duyvil|url=https://www.nypl.org/blog/2010/04/29/history-name-spuyten-duyvil|access-date=2 January 2017|work=[[New York Public Library]]|date=April 29, 2010}}</ref> Historian [[Reginald Pelham Bolton]], however, argues that the phrase means "spouting meadow", referring to a fresh-water spring at Inwood Hill.<ref>Selyns, Henricus. [https://books.google.com/books?id=9mhCAQAAIAAJ&q=%22spuyten+duyvil%22+%22spouting+meadow%22+bolton ''Liber A: 1628-1700 of the Collegiate Churches of New York''], p. 319. [[William B. Eerdmans Publishing Company]], 2009. {{ISBN|9780802865090}}. Accessed November 24, 2020. "In an attempt at giving a historically accurate etymology, Reginald Pelham Bolton maintains that the Dutch name ''Spuyten Duyvil'' (the present spelling) is a topographic designation, referring to a spring near Inwood Hill, and meaning 'spouting meadow'"</ref><ref>Sypher, Frank J. [https://www.nytimes.com/1993/11/14/nyregion/l-dispute-springs-eternal-over-spuyten-duyvil-032093.html "Dispute Springs Eternal Over 'Spuyten Duyvil'" (letter to the editor)] ''[[The New York Times]]'', November 14, 1993. Accessed November 24, 2020. "Reginald Pelham Bolton, in his authoritative history, ''Washington Heights'' (1924), argues persuasively that the Dutch name actually means 'sprouting meadow,' referring to the beautiful spring that to this day rises at the foot of Inwood Hill, near what remains of the original course of the Spuyten Duyvil Creek.... Correction: Nov. 21, 1993... It should have read 'spouting meadow,' not 'sprouting meadow.'"</ref>

An additional translation, "to spite the Devil" or "in spite of the devil", was popularized by a story in [[Washington Irving]]'s ''[[A History of New York|A Knickerbocker's History of New York]]'' published in 1809. Set in the 1660s, the story tells of trumpeter [[Anthony Van Corlaer|Antony Van Corlear]] summoned by "Peter de Groodt" to warn settlers of an attempted British invasion, with Corlear attempting to swim across the "[[Harlem River|Harlean river"]] from Fort Amsterdam to the Bronx mainland "in spite of the devil (spyt den duyvel)", Irving writes. The treacherous current pulled him under and he lost his life. This resulted in the name "Spuyten Duyvil" for "the adjoining promontory, which projects into the Hudson."<ref>[[Washington Irving|Irving, Washington]] (2004) [1809]  [https://www.gutenberg.org/files/13042/13042-h/13042-h.htm ''Knickerbocker's History of New York, Complete''] [[Project Gutenberg]]. Book VII, Chapter X.</ref><ref name="NYCPks-SpuytenDuyvilCrk"/><ref name="NYPL-SpuytenDuyvil-Ap2010"/><ref name=boland2002>{{cite news |title=F.Y.I. – Beating the Devil |last=Boland Jr.|first=Ed |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=October 13, 2002 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/10/13/nyregion/fyi-331902.html?pagewanted=1}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Baumstone|first1=Hal|title=Stanford News: Legend or History|url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/viewer/?file=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%25206%2FPine%2520Plaines%2520NY%2520Register%2520Herald%2FPine%2520Plaines%2520NY%2520Register%2520Herald%25201988%2520Grayscale.pdf%2FPine%2520Plaines%2520NY%2520Register%2520Herald%25201988%2520Grayscalte%2520-%25200100.pdf&highlightsFile=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2Fhighlighter%2Fhits%2Ff90610c4ae931a46f4e7f7a7a9351e79#page=1|access-date=2 January 2017|work=Pine Plains Register Herald|agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]]|date=January 28, 1988|page=8}}</ref>

An extensive appendix to ''Studies in Etymology and Etiology'' (2009) by David L. Gold, which includes commentary by Rob Rentenaar, professor of [[onomastics]] at the [[University of Amsterdam]], goes into great detail about all the various translations for "Spuyten Duyvil" which have been mooted over the years.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gold |first1=David L. |title=Studies in Etymology and Etiology: With Emphasis on Germanic, Jewish, Romance and Slavic Languages |date=2009 |publisher=Universidad de Alicante |isbn=978-84-7908-517-9 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=l015C5vm1XkC&q=Spuyten%20Duyvil&pg=PA122 |language=en}}</ref> Rentenaar concludes that "Duyvil" means "devil", either literally or in a transferred sense, but he could not determine what the intended meaning of "Spuyten" was because of the many variants that have been used throughout history.<ref>Gold, David L. and Rentenaar, Rob "Appendix 1: On the Etymology of the New York City Place Names ''Gramercy Park'', ''Hell Gate'', and ''Spuyten Duyvil'', the New Jersey Place Name ''Barnegat'', and Regional American English ''Fly ~ Vlei ~ Vley ~ Vlaie ~ Vly'' in Gold, David L. (2009) ''Studies in Etymology and Etiology: With Emphasis on Germanic, Jewish, Romance and Slavic Languages''. Universidad de Alicante.    [https://books.google.com/books?id=l015C5vm1XkC&q=Spuyten%20Duyvil&pg=PA145 pp.145-146] {{isbn|978-8-47-90851-79}}</ref>

The creek was referred to as ''Shorakapok'' by [[Lenape]] Native Americans in the area, translated as "the sitting-down place" or "the place between the ridges".<ref name="NYCPks-SpuytenDuyvilCrk"/>

==History==

In the late 17th century, [[Frederick Philipse]], the lord of [[Philipse Manor Hall State Historic Site|Philipse Manor]] in Westchester County, received permission to construct a bridge across Spuyten Duyvil Creek and charge tolls.  "King's Bridge", which was located roughly south of and parallel to where West 230th Street lies today, opened in 1693.{{sfn|Burrows|Wallace|1999|p=100}}

Development of the neighborhood began in the latter half of the 19th century once the [[New York Central and Hudson River Railroad]] came through.<ref name=encnyc />  The tracks originally crossed Spuyten Duyvil Creek and into Manhattan on the west side, but [[Cornelius Vanderbilt]] wanted to consolidate his railroad operations into one terminal, so he had tracks laid along the north side of the Harlem River so that trains coming south from Albany could join with the Harlem and New Haven lines and come into Manhattan down [[Fourth Avenue (Manhattan)|Fourth Avenue]] into his new [[Grand Central Depot]].{{sfn|Burrows|Wallace|1999|p=944}} This is the route still used by [[Metro-North]] today.

Through the 1920s development of the Spuyten Duyvil neighborhood continued. Large high-rise apartment buildings, which later became [[condominium]]s and [[cooperative housing|cooperatives]], began to be built in the 1950s and continued through the 1980s, bringing in affluent families attracted by its scenic qualities, as well as by the area's closeness to desirable neighborhoods such as [[Fieldston, Bronx|Fieldston]] and [[Riverdale, Bronx|Riverdale]].<ref name=encnyc />

[[File:Henry Hudson column jeh top.JPG|left|175px|thumb|Statue of [[Henry Hudson]] on top of a tall column at [[Henry Hudson Park]] in Spuyten Duyvil]]

On July 18, 2013, [[July 2013 Spuyten Duyvil derailment|a freight train derailed]] near the [[Spuyten Duyvil (Metro-North station)|Spuyten Duyvil station]] due to an excessively wide [[track gauge|gauge]] at one point. No one was killed or injured.<ref>{{cite web|title=Railroad Accident Brief: Metro-North Railroad Derailment|url=https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/AccidentReports/Reports/RAB1411.pdf|publisher=[[National Transportation Safety Board]]|date=October 24, 2014|access-date=May 24, 2015}}</ref> Less than six months later, on December 1, [[December 2013 Spuyten Duyvil derailment|a commuter train derailment]] near the Spuyten Duyvil station resulted in 4 deaths and over 70 injuries, 11 of them critical.<ref>{{cite web | last1=Barron | first1=James | last2=Goodman | first2=J. David | title=Focus Turns to Investigation in Fatal Bronx Train Crash | website=The New York Times | date=2013-12-01 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/12/02/nyregion/metro-north-derailment.html | access-date=2017-01-02}}</ref> The cause of the second derailment was determined to be excessive speed.<ref>{{cite web | title=Attorney: Metro-North train engineer was 'in a daze' | website=ABC7 New York | date=2013-12-04 | url=http://abc7ny.com/archive/9344996/ | access-date=2017-01-02}}</ref>

==Demographics==
Based on data from the [[2010 United States census]], the population of [[Kingsbridge, Bronx|Kingsbridge]] and Spuyten Duyvil was 30,161, a change of 289 (1%) from the 29,872 counted in [[2000 United States census|2000]]. Covering an area of {{convert|540.92|acres}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{convert|55.8|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name=PLP5>[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf Table PL-P5 NTA: Total Population and Persons Per Acre - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010], Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. Accessed June 16, 2016.</ref>

The racial makeup of the neighborhoods were 49.3% (14,872) [[White (U.S. Census)|White]], 8.9% (2,691) [[African American (U.S. Census)|African American]], 0.1% (40) [[Native American (U.S. Census)|Native American]], 5.7% (1,731) [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 0% (15) [[Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)|Pacific Islander]], 0.3% (98) from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 1.7% (510) from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race were 33.8% (10,204) of the population.<ref name=PLP3A>[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf Table PL-P3A NTA: Total Population by Mutually Exclusive Race and Hispanic Origin - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010], Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, March 29, 2011. Accessed June 14, 2016.</ref>

A restaurant guide once described the neighborhood as "[[upper middle class]]".<ref>Rossi, Roberto (2018) [https://books.google.com/books?id=r5CNDwAAQBAJ&dq=%22Spuyten%20Duyvil%22%20%22upper%20middle%22&pg=PT146 ''A Vegan's Guide to New York City'']</ref>

==Police and crime==
Spuyten Duyvil is patrolled by the 50th Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]], located at 3450 Kingsbridge Avenue.<ref name="NYPD 50th Precinct">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/50th-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 50th Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref> The 50th Precinct ranked 13th safest out of 69 patrol areas for per-capita crime in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/bronx/riverdale/|title=Riverdale: Marble Hill, Fieldston, Spuyten Duyvil, Kingsbridge – DNAinfo.com Crime and Safety Report|website=www.dnainfo.com|access-date=October 6, 2016|archive-date=April 15, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170415053338/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/bronx/riverdale|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The 50th Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 69.9% between 1990 and 2022. The precinct reported three murders, 22 rapes, 185 robberies, 213 felony assaults, 126 burglaries, 695 grand larcenies, and 288 grand larcenies auto in 2022.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-050pct.pdf|title=50th Precinct CompStat Report|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=July 22, 2018}}</ref>

==Library==
The [[New York Public Library]] (NYPL) operates the Spuyten Duyvil branch at 650 West 235th Street. The one-story branch opened in 1971 and was designed by [[Giorgio Cavaglieri]].<ref>{{cite web | title=About the Spuyten Duyvil Library | website=The New York Public Library | url=https://www.nypl.org/about/locations/spuyten-duyvil | access-date=March 14, 2019}}</ref>

[[File:Spuyten Duyvil train station.jpg|thumb|300px|right|The Spuyten Duyvil train station with Henry Hudson Bridge above]]

==Transportation==

The following [[MTA Regional Bus Operations]] bus routes serve Spuyten Duyvil:<ref name=busbx>{{cite NYC bus map|Bx}}</ref>

* [[Bx1 (New York City bus)|Bx1]]: to [[Third Avenue–138th Street (IRT Pelham Line)|Third Avenue–138th Street]] station (via [[Grand Concourse (Bronx)|Grand Concourse]])
* [[Bx7 (New York City bus)|Bx7]]: to [[168th Street (New York City Subway)|168th Street]] station, Manhattan (via Riverdale Avenue, and Broadway)
* [[Bx10 (New York City bus)|Bx10]]: to [[Norwood–205th Street (IND Concourse Line)|Norwood–205th Street]] station (via Riverdale Avenue, Henry Hudson Parkway, and Johnson Avenue)
* [[Bx20 (New York City bus)|Bx20]]: to [[Inwood–207th Street (IND Eighth Avenue Line)|Inwood–207th Street]] station, Manhattan (via Henry Hudson Parkway, and Johnson Avenue)

Spuyten Duyvil is the location of the [[Spuyten Duyvil (Metro-North station)|Spuyten Duyvil train station]], which is served by the [[Hudson Line (Metro-North)|Hudson Line]] of the [[Metro-North Railroad]], providing service into [[Grand Central Terminal]] and north into [[Westchester County, New York|Westchester County]]. [[Spuyten Duyvil Bridge]], a railroad swing bridge that carries [[Amtrak]]'s [[Empire Corridor]] line between New York City and [[Albany, New York|Albany]], spans Spuyten Duyvil Creek. The north end of the [[Henry Hudson Bridge]] connects the neighborhood to the island of [[Manhattan]] via the [[Henry Hudson Parkway]].

[[Hudson Rail Link]] connects the Metro-North station to the surrounding area, with [[Hudson Rail Link#Routes|Routes J, K, L, and M]] serving Spuyten Duyvil.

==Points of interest==
*'''[[Edgehill Church of Spuyten Duyvil]]''' (former [[United Church of Christ]]) was built in 1888–89 as a chapel of the [[Riverdale Presbyterian Church Complex|Riverdale Presbyterian Church]] located nearby, for the use of workers at the giant Johnson Iron Foundry which was located nearby at the time. It was designed by [[Francis H. Kimball]] in an eclectic mix of styles: [[Romanesque Revival architecture|Romanesque Revival]], [[Tudor Revival architecture|Tudor Revival]] and [[Shingle style architecture|Shingle style]]. The church was designated a [[New York City landmark]] in 1980. As of 2022, the church has closed, and the building is the headquarters of the Kingsbridge Historical Society, the oldest historical society in the Bronx.<ref name=aia /><ref name=nycland>{{harvnb|New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission|Dolkart|Postal|2009|p=346}}</ref>
*'''[[Henry Hudson Park|Henry Hudson Memorial Park]]''' features the '''Henry Hudson Monument''', a {{convert|16|ft|m|adj=on}} bronze statue of [[Henry Hudson]] sculpted by [[Karl Bitter]] and Karl Gruppe on top of a {{convert|100|ft|m|adj=on}} [[Doric column]] by architect Walter Cook of the firm of [[Babb, Cook & Willard]]. The column was raised by public subscription c.1912 after the [[Hudson-Fulton Celebration]] of 1909, but the project stalled when  funds ran out, and Bitter died in 1915.  The ''Heroic statue of Henry Hudson'' was redesigned and completed by Gruppe – a student of Bitter – based on Bitter's plaster model. It was added by [[Robert Moses]]' [[Henry Hudson Parkway|Henry Hudson Parkway Authority]] in 1938, along with the two [[bas-relief]] panels at the column's base, also by Gruppe.  The south panel shows Hudson receiving his commission from the [[Dutch East India Company]], and the north panel shows Native Americans and Europeans at the first Dutch trading post on Manhattan Island.  The monument was dedicated on January 6, 1938.<ref name=encnyc /><ref name=aia5 /><ref>Informational sign on site</ref>
*{{anchor|Villa Charlotte Bronte}}'''Villa Charlotte Brontë''' is a [[co-op apartment]] complex of two small three-story buildings at 2501 Palisade Avenue, containing 17 units, each with a different floor plan. It was built in 1926 and designed by Robert W. Gardner in the style of an [[Italian Villa style|Italian villa]] for attorney, developer and preservationist [[John Jay McKelvey Sr.]]{{efn|Gardner also designed the Staten Island Institute of Arts and Sciences, which became the [[Staten Island Museum]].}}  Similar in concept to [[apartment#Garden apartment (US)|garden apartments]], it is regarded as one of the first apartment buildings in the Bronx.  The complex overlooks the Hudson River – McKelvey advertised the apartments in ''[[The New York Times]]'', as being for anyone whose "soul is hungry for the majesty of the river" – and many of the apartments have views of [[The Palisades (Hudson River)|the Palisades]] in New Jersey.  The building is not landmarked, and a companion building, the seven-apartment cottage-like Villa Rosa Bonheur at 2395 Palisade Avenue, built in 1924, was torn down in 2019 after failing as a co-op in 1941. It kept on as a private home for decades afterwards until it was sold to a developer, who replaced it with an undistinguished apartment building, to the distress of the neighborhood. Villa Victoria (1927), a more ordinary [[Tudor Revival architecture|Tudor-style]] apartment building, located between the other two "villas", still remains standing at 2475 Palisade Avenue, although McKelvey did lose possession of it in a foreclosure.<ref name=aia5>{{cite aia5|page=868}}</ref><ref>[[Christopher Gray (architectural historian)|Gray, Christopher]] (October 22, 2006) [https://www.nytimes.com/2006/10/22/realestate/22scap.html "Streetscapes: Two Picturesque Buildings With River Views to Match"] ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref><ref>Santoro, Lisa M. (June 1, 2016) [https://web.archive.org/web/20160602113834/http://ny.curbed.com/2016/6/1/11828788/the-history-of-villa-charlotte-bronte-a-romantic-idyll-in-the-bronx "The History of Villa Charlotte Bronte, a Romantic Idyll in the Bronx"] ''[[Curbed|Curbed New York]]''</ref><ref>Bady, David (ndg) [https://www.lehman.edu/vpadvance/artgallery/arch/buildings/bronte.html "Villa Charlotte Bronte"] [[Lehman College]] Art Gallery/Architecture</ref><ref>Kris (June 14, 2022) [https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/villa-charlotte-bronte "Villa Charlotte Bronte"] ''Atlas Obscura''</ref><ref>Staff (April 28, 2025) [https://ephemeralnewyork.wordpress.com/2025/04/28/the-story-of-the-villa-charlotte-bronte-a-magical-1920s-cliffside-co-op-high-above-the-hudson/ "The story of the Villa Charlotte Bronte, a magical 1920s cliffside co-op high above the Hudson"] ''Ephemeral New York''</ref>{{clear left}}
